opus-5.5.text:
I think intuition for neural networks is built mostly by hands-on work rather than by reading. When I started, I read the papers, looked at the equations for attention, and felt I understood it. That understanding was quite shallow. It only became real once I had trained models myself, watched them fail, and had to work out why.

For me the process has a few layers.

**The first layer is mechanical.** You need to know what each component is actually doing. In a transformer, attention is a way for each token to decide which other tokens to pull information from. The MLP layers act more like a key-value memory that stores and transforms features. The residual stream is a shared communication channel that every layer reads from and writes to. Once you hold that picture in your head, a lot of behavior stops looking mysterious. For example, you can ask what information a given layer could plausibly have access to at that point, and the answer is often informative.

**The second layer comes from experiments, especially ones that surprise you.** You form a hypothesis, maybe that a certain data change will help or that the model is relying on some shortcut feature. You run it, and very often you're wrong. Those moments are the most valuable, because each one corrects your mental model a little. Over time you accumulate many small corrections, and that accumulation is what people call intuition. I'd say intuition is mostly compressed experience of being wrong.

**The third layer is about scale and data.** Many intuitions from small models don't transfer. Things that look like hard limitations at small scale sometimes simply disappear with more parameters or better data. Other behaviors only emerge once the model is large enough. So part of good intuition is a healthy humility: you keep asking whether what you're seeing is a fundamental property or an artifact of the regime you happen to be in. I've come to believe data matters more than most architectural tweaks. A lot of what a model "knows" or how it "behaves" is really a reflection of what it saw during training.

**The last layer is learning to look at the model from the inside.** Probing activations, looking at attention patterns, ablating components, studying what happens when you perturb inputs. Some of this is interpretability work, some is just debugging. You start to treat the model less like a black box and more like a system you can poke at and reason about, almost like a biologist with an organism.

If I had to give advice to someone starting out, I'd say: train small models from scratch, keep the feedback loop fast, and write down your predictions before you run things. Then compare. That habit of predicting and checking is, I think, the fastest way to build real intuition, rather than an illusion of understanding that comes from reading explanations.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition as accumulating through repeated experiments and corrections over time, but it does not distinguish that gradual process from sudden insight.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think intuition for these systems isn't something you develop by reading papers. You develop it by getting your hands dirty, and mostly by being wrong a lot.

When I first started working with transformers, I had this very clean mental picture from the architecture diagrams. Attention, feed-forward, residual connections, layer norm. I could explain every block. But I had no feel for it. I couldn't look at a training curve and tell you why it plateaued, or look at a model's output and guess which component was responsible. That kind of knowledge only came after I'd trained many models myself, broken them in many different ways, and stared at the failures.

So the first stage, for me, is building the thing from scratch. Not using a library, actually writing the attention mechanism, actually watching the loss go down. You realize very quickly that the math on paper and the behavior in practice are quite different. Small things matter enormously. Initialization, learning rate warmup, how you normalize. Those aren't details in the textbook sense. They're the whole game sometimes.

The second stage is running lots of small experiments and forming hypotheses. You start to notice patterns. Like, when a model memorizes rather than generalizes, the loss curve has a particular shape. When attention heads specialize, you can almost predict which layers it'll happen in. You build a kind of internal simulator. Before you run the experiment, you make a guess, and then you check. Over time, your guesses get better. That's really what intuition is, I think. It's a compressed version of hundreds of experiments you've already done.

The third thing, and this is maybe less obvious, is that you have to let go of the idea that there's a single correct intuition. Different people have different useful mental models. Some people think of attention as soft lookup, some think of it as routing information, some think in terms of circuits. None of these is complete. But each of them is useful for certain problems. The skill is knowing which lens to pick up for which question.

And I'd add one more thing. Intuition has a shelf life. What I believed about scaling three years ago, some of it turned out to be wrong. The field moves, the models change, and you have to keep updating. So I try to hold my intuitions loosely. They're tools, not beliefs. If an experiment contradicts what I expected, that's the most interesting moment, because that's exactly where my model of the world has a hole in it.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition developing through many experiments and improving over time, but it does not distinguish that process from sudden insight.

astra-6.text:
I think intuition develops through a cycle of making predictions, running experiments, and figuring out why you were wrong. You can read an explanation and feel that you understand it, but the stronger test is whether you can anticipate what a model will do when you change something.

For neural networks, I’d start with something small enough to inspect. Look at the activations, the gradients, and how the loss changes during training. If training stalls, can you explain why? As you connect the equations to those observations, the equations become less abstract.

With transformers, it helps to follow a token through the computation. What information can it access through attention? What happens through the residual connections and the feed-forward layers? Then implement a small version and test your understanding. For example, what would happen if you removed positional information? Make a prediction before you run it.

I also think you need to be careful with intuitive stories. Saying that attention ‘finds relevant information’ is useful initially, but it doesn’t explain every behavior of a trained model. Good intuition includes knowing where your explanation stops working. For me, that’s the process: build a simple mental model, confront it with actual behavior, and gradually refine it.

r001.rationale: The response describes intuition as developing gradually through experiments and refinement, but it does not distinguish sudden insight from understanding that takes an extended period to develop.

sol-6.1.text:
I think intuition develops through a loop: you study the mechanism, make a prediction about how it behaves, and then check that prediction with an experiment. When the result surprises you, that’s often where you learn the most.

For neural networks, I’d start with a small model and really understand what changes during training. What happens if you change the activation function, the learning rate, or the amount of data? Equations give you one view, but watching the loss and inspecting the representations gives you another.

With transformers, it helps to follow a single token through the computation. What information can it access through attention? How does that information get mixed into its representation? Then you can connect those operations to behavior you observe in the model.

The important thing is to keep your intuition testable. Being able to tell a convincing story about why a model works isn’t quite the same as being able to predict what it will do. I think the second ability is what you want to develop.

r001.rationale: The response describes developing intuition through study, prediction, and experimentation, but it does not distinguish sudden insight from understanding that takes an extended period to develop.
